title: Indian-American Lawmakers Join 63 in Congress Urging Faster Green Cards as Health Coverage Lapses
excerpt: A letter led by Reps. Clarke and Grijalva asks USCIS Director Joseph Edlow for an emergency I-485 expedite pathway after October 1 healthcare cuts left legally present immigrants uninsured while their green cards wait.
body:
• Sixty-three members of Congress, including Indian-American lawmakers Raja Krishnamoorthi, Pramila Jayapal and Shri Thanedar, have asked USCIS to fast-track green cards for legally present immigrants losing health coverage.
  • New eligibility limits under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act took effect on October 1 and cut Medicaid, CHIP, Medicare and Affordable Care Act help for refugees, asylees and other lawfully present groups who do not yet hold a green card.
  • The lawmakers cite more than 281,000 people in nine states and Washington, DC, facing Medicaid loss from October 1, and a Congressional Budget Office estimate of 1.4 million uninsured by 2034.
  • If your Form I-485 is pending and your coverage has ended, you can request an expedite today at no fee via the USCIS Contact Center at 800-375-5283, under urgent humanitarian or severe financial loss grounds.

Sixty-three members of Congress have urged US Citizenship and Immigration Services to expedite green-card applications for legally present immigrants who are losing government-funded healthcare while their cases wait for a decision. The letter, dated October 14 and released publicly on October 19, was addressed to USCIS Director Joseph B. Edlow and led by Democratic Representatives Yvette D. Clarke of New York and Adelita S. Grijalva of Arizona, according to hi INDiA's report of the IANS wire. Indian-American lawmakers Raja Krishnamoorthi, Pramila Jayapal and Shri Thanedar were among the 61 other signatories.

Coverage ended on October 1, before the green cards arrived

Restrictions under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act took effect on October 1 and narrowed eligibility for Medicaid, the Children's Health Insurance Program, Medicare and Affordable Care Act premium tax credits. Refugees, asylum recipients and survivors of domestic violence and human trafficking are among the groups affected. Many of them would qualify for continued benefits as lawful permanent residents, the lawmakers argue, but their permanent residence applications remain pending.

https://x.com/TheSiasatDaily/status/2112390059366244736

The letter cites the case of an Arizona woman with stage-four metastatic breast cancer who lost Medicaid coverage on October 1. She is legally present, depends on chemotherapy, and her green-card application is still pending. Grijalva said more than 20,000 legally present refugees and immigrants in Arizona are at risk, pointing also to a nine-year-old boy with epilepsy. The congressional release put the number facing Medicaid loss from October 1 at more than 281,000 people across nine states and Washington, DC, and cited a Congressional Budget Office estimate that 1.4 million legally present immigrants could become uninsured nationwide by 2034.

Three specific asks of USCIS

The lawmakers requested three immediate measures, as detailed in Immigration Analytics' breakdown of the letter. First, an emergency expedited processing pathway for I-485 applicants facing imminent healthcare termination. Second, clarification of the expedite criteria, explicitly naming loss of health coverage as an expedite ground. Third, coordination between USCIS, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services and state agencies so coverage terminations could be delayed while applications remain pending.

"Needless red tape should never be the determinant between life and death."

— Rep. Yvette D. Clarke

Why an expedite may not reach the people most affected

Part of what the letter seeks already exists on paper. The USCIS Policy Manual allows the agency to expedite a case for severe financial loss, urgent humanitarian reasons, compelling US government interests or clear USCIS error. A patient about to lose coverage for cancer treatment can already ask under the humanitarian ground, but the decision rests in USCIS's sole discretion. Written criteria naming coverage loss would make outcomes more predictable.

For refugees, there is a second obstacle. On November 21, 2025, Edlow ordered a review of refugees admitted between January 20, 2021 and February 20, 2025, and placed their pending green-card applications on hold, according to the memo as reported by the Associated Press and CBS News. An expedite moves a case up the queue; it does not lift a policy hold. USCIS figures underline the effect: the agency completed 3,805 refugee adjustment applications in the first nine months of fiscal 2026, down from 37,908 in the same period a year earlier.

What readers with a pending I-485 can do now

USCIS controls processing speed, not health eligibility, which is why the letter's third request is for coordination rather than a USCIS ruling on coverage. There is no premium processing for Form I-485 and no fee to request an expedite, but the bar is high and evidence is essential, as LegalClarity's guide to I-485 expediting options explains. Requests start with the USCIS Contact Center at 800-375-5283 or the Emma assistant on the USCIS website, with a receipt number ready and documents such as medical records or termination notices to follow. The next pressure point is January 1, 2027, when Marketplace premium subsidies end for many of the same immigrants who lack a green card. USCIS has not yet agreed to the requests.
